stemMd: Which of the following developments most closely parallels the pattern described in the final paragraph of the passage?
instructionsMd: Answer on the basis of the passage only.

options.label: A
options.textMd: A government requires every manufacturer to adopt a new plug design, after which households gradually replace their appliances.

options.label: B
options.textMd: A file format first used by printing firms that need exact reproduction becomes common in ordinary offices, and a government later specifies it for official documents.

options.label: C
options.textMd: An industry association withdraws a standard after its members complain that it is inconvenient to follow.

options.label: D
options.textMd: Two competing measurement systems stay in everyday use for decades because neither offers users a clear advantage.

explanationMd:
State the pattern in the final paragraph in general terms. A standard (1) is adopted first by the users who most need precise coordination, (2) spreads to others because following it is convenient, and (3) is only later written into law, which "recorded a change that had already happened". The key feature is the order: adoption by need, then convenience, then law.

The file format matches all three steps: specialist users who need exactness, spread to ordinary offices, and a later government specification.

**How to check.** Test each option against the order of events. The plug example puts the law first, which is precisely what the passage says did NOT happen. The two-systems example has no standard becoming dominant at all. The withdrawn standard fails to spread.

distractorRationale.a: Here the rule is imposed first and practice follows. The passage's point is the reverse: the standard became dominant "without being imposed", and the law came afterwards.
distractorRationale.d: Nothing becomes dominant here. The passage does describe a period when two times coexisted, but its final paragraph is about how one standard came to prevail.
distractorRationale.c: A standard that is abandoned because it is inconvenient is the opposite of one that spreads because "others found it convenient to follow".

accessibilityText: A question about the passage on railway time. It asks which development most closely parallels the final paragraph's pattern, in which a standard is adopted first by those needing precise coordination, spreads by convenience, and is later recorded in law. The options are: a file format used first by printing firms spreads to offices and is later specified by government; a government mandates a plug design and households follow; two systems coexist for decades; an association withdraws an inconvenient standard.

provenance.notes: Original parallel-reasoning item. The key reproduces the order of events; distractors reverse it, lack a dominant standard, or lack spread.
